utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we start, I have a few preliminaries. The first one being that the statement on bar table motions which was already distributed among the parties, at least a courtesy copy, still has to be read into the record, which I'll start to do now. The Chamber will now address the issue of the upcoming bar table motions by the Stanisic Defence. On the 21st of November, 2011, the Stanisic Defence notified the Chamber informally that it intended to a file a bar table motion. This matter was subsequently discussed in court, including on the 24th of November and the 7th of December, in 2011, when the Stanisic Defence clarified that it intended to file three bar table motions, two of which covered some 800 documents. On the 7th of December, the Chamber expressed concern about such major bar table motions being filed at a relatively late stage of the trial and asked the parties to meet and try to reach an agreement with regard to some of the subject matter covered by the documents. On the 13th of January, 2012, the parties updated the Chamber informally on the state of their discussions. The Chamber will make a number of observations in this respect. As mentioned, the Stanisic Defence has indicated that the bar table motions would tender at least 800 documents for admission into evidence. The Chamber notes that the total number of Defence exhibits tendered by the -- by both Defence teams, at present, is around 650 documents. The Chamber further notes that the Stanisic Defence case is, too a large extent, over and the proceedings in this case are drawing to a close. When the Prosecution, during its case, submitted a bar table motion covering a large number of document, the Chamber expressed its concerns about being flooded by hundreds of documents without precise information about how they would fit into the tendering party's case. The Chamber further emphasised that it would prefer to receive evidence through witnesses. This can be found on transcript pages 3685 through 3690. These considerations apply equally to the presentation of evidence in the Defence cases. In cases before this Tribunal, where there is an enormous amount of potential evidentiary material that can be considered relevant and of probative value, the burden falls heavily on the parties to organise the presentation of their evidence in such a way that the Chamber is able to properly consider it. It is for the parties to carefully select the most relevant and probative documents and to provide a clear indication as to the documents' place within the wider case and the party's purpose in tendering them. Not doing this creates a practical and organisational problem for any responding parties and for the Chamber. More importantly, however, the party runs the risk that the Chamber will not be able to consider that piece of evidence in the way the party intended. In this respect, the Chamber notes that a document can be relied on to establish a number of different fact, only some of which are obvious at first glance. For example, a government report describing a series of events can be used to establish that a specific governmental institution had information that these events took place. However, the same document might be used to establish that the institution took action in response to the events. In addition, or alternatively, the report can be used to demonstrate that the series of events in fact took place. On the other hand, the tendering party might only have intended for the document to prove that the author of the report worked at the governmental institution at that time. The Chamber expects the party tendering such a document to indicate precisely which information contained in the document it seeks to rely on. When a document is tendered through a witness, the tendering party's line of questioning and the witness's testimony provide a certain amount of context to the document. When a document is bar tabled, however, it is for the tendering party to explain the context in detail. The Chamber notes that the parties have made some progress regarding the possible future bar table motions by the Stanisic Defence. In particular, in paragraphs 5 and 7 of the informal communication of the 13th of January, 2012, the parties indicate that some of the documentation is being transformed into agreed facts. The Chamber welcomes this. In the informal communication, the parties indicate that there might be disagreement about what conclusions to draw from particular documents. However, such disagreements should not be an obstacle to agree on the content of the documents. The parties could address the interpretation of and conclusions to be drawn from specific documents separately; for example, in their final briefs. Considering the size of possible future bar table motions and the stage of the proceedings, the Chamber expects the parties to treat this issue as a priority. Once a bar table motion is submitted, the other parties need time to respond, and the Chamber needs time to consider it. The Chamber expects the first concrete steps by the 17th of February, 2012, either in the form of a record of agreed facts and/or in the form of a bar table motion tendering those documents on which no agreement could be reached. These first steps do not have to deal with all of the documents, and the Chamber will set further deadlines in due course. Considering that the parties have already discussed the documents in depth, the Chamber expects responses by the parties to any such motion not later than the 2nd of March, 2012. As the parties are aware, this is a departure from the Chamber's guidance on bar table motions of the 7th of July, 2009, which foresees a joint filing. And this concludes the Chamber's statement. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's slightly -- it's slightly unfortunate timing, but we are going to disclose another bar table to the Prosecution today. And I say unfortunate timing because it will probably not make me very popular. But there are 330 documents within that bar table, and in some senses it's the largest bar table because it contains many of the governmental-type minutes which we'd like to rely upon. I raise it now simply just to -- in the spirit of candor. In light of Your Honour's guidance, we'll do what we can to -- with the Prosecution to reduce that. But we do see some fairly intractable problems with trying to reduce these types of minutes to -- in line with Your Honours's guidance. But obviously we'll do our best and we do appreciate the guidance and what it's trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're talking about the minutes, I think the first step should be that -- to find the relevant parts of those minutes, because usually minutes of meetings cover far more subjects than perhaps relevant for the party to tender that portion of the minutes. But we'll first leave it to the parties to see -- and, of course, finally, there are -- filing a motion and agreeing or trying to reach an agreement with the Prosecution is the first step to, I would say, to enhance the possibility that the tendering will be successful, that is, leads to admission of the documents into admission. Because, that's, of course, the second step.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is important for the tendering party, and I can imagine that selection and self-restriction may enhance the chances of success if we're talking about these amounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I mean, on one view -- well my preliminary view is that it may well be useful to have a short hearing on the subject, because I can see that we are going to hit an impasse. And the impasse will be that which has been indicated to Your Honours, which -- and resolves around notice, something that, as Your Honours know, I've been talking for many, many a month. And I put it like that, because if I just take the governmental-type minutes, the governmental-type minutes often tell a very detailed story about who was making decisions, the type of decisions being made, the type of supplies from, for example, the Serbian government or the FRY to the Bosnian Serbs, and it is, from our perspective, very difficult to remove much of that and just take the highlights, in the absence of the Prosecution indicating with greater clarity what their case is. If their case is as they advance -- have advanced it so far, these accused were responsible for pretty much everything, and they were the ones guiding and controlling everything. It's very difficult then to have in our possession documents from government meetings showing that there are many other people who are the front runners in that -- on that issue but then be asked to reduce or take away some of that evidence. If the Prosecution would supply greater precision, then -- instead of alleging everything, then we might be able to get somewhere a bit more swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your proposal was to have a short hearing on the matter. You started already, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that. I take it that the parties -- first that you'll indicate to the Prosecution what that material is. And let's not anticipate on getting stuck on matters where apparently the discussion has not started yet. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I just wanted to add, before we express our view or anything on a proposed hearing, following the Chamber's statement we are going to be sending informal communication to the Stanisic Defence, basically giving them our current position and our view, asking them a few questions. Based on their response, we will then send information to the Chamber as to what we believe from our position our current view is. I think with that information, Your Honours, the Chamber will be in a position to assess perhaps what next steps need to be taken in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Then the second item on my agenda are the leftovers of tendering of documents from last week, Witness Pelevic. There were some problems with the format of video materials, et cetera. We were running out of time. Could the parties inform me what material, hopefully properly uploaded in the e-court, is still there to be tendered. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution had two videos in that regard of note. One was 2D1001, which I believe was displayed during the Simatovic examination, related to the five-minute speech of Arkan's -- including the text of the "united states of Serbia." The second one was a Prosecution video, 65 ter 6316, which had not been uploaded at the time that it was displayed, which was two video-clips from the funeral proceedings of Radovan Stojicic, Badza. The Prosecution also used a still with the witness, 65 ter 6316.1, which was related to that video. Aside from that, we did have three other exhibits that were marked for identification that we would be seeking to tender again; that's P307--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's take it one by one. Let's first focus on the videos. 2D1001, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P3073, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? P3073 is admitted into evidence. The other video, 65 ter 6316, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P3074, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? P3074 is admitted into evidence. The still from that video, 6316.1, or is that included, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will P3075, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. P3075 is admitted into evidence. Then the three --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- documents marked for identification. These were -- could you please briefly refer to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. The three that the Prosecution had of record, they were carry-overs from the end of the cross-examination of Mr. Pelevic, were documents produced by Mr. Pelevic to the Simatovic Defence but then the Prosecution examined Mr. Pelevic upon towards the latter part of the day. They're exhibits P3070, which is a form related to an individual by the name of Zarka Radnov; P3071, which is a form related to Aleksandar Manojlovic; and P3072, which was a certificate that was pertaining to an individual by the last name of Velickovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against admission? Not. P3070, P3071, and P3072 are admitted into evidence. Nothing else remaining?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then all on the record. Mr. Jordash, the -- during the 26th of January proceedings, the Prosecution proposed that an investigator from its Belgrade office go to the home of Witness Pelevic to photograph a board of photographs at the witness's home, and the Stanisic Defence objected, linking its objection to its submissions that the Prosecution violated Rule 90(H)(ii) in its cross-examination of the witness. Now, that objection was followed by some additional questions put by the Chamber to the witness and some questions you wanted to put to the witness, which creates a situation which is at least slightly different from the situation when you made these observations. The first question I would have is whether you are still seeking a ruling on your Rule 90(H)(ii) objections in light of these subsequent questions which were very much focussing on the Prosecution's case. Could I hear whether you still, now knowing what the answers of the witness have been, whether you still --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't seek a ruling at this point, but we say that without prejudice to submissions we'd like to or may make at the closing stage concerning what the Prosecution, in our view, should have put to that witness. We -- we appreciated the course that Your Honours took, but Your Honours will also appreciate that the time was extremely limited, and I'd like to be able to look at, again, how the Prosecution proceeded with the witness, and what they may seek to rely upon in the future and what our position would be in they do seek to rely upon certain aspects of his evidence without having, in our view, put their case very clearly. So we don't ask for a ruling, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now, of course, Mr. Jordash, I will discuss it with my colleagues, but at a certain moment it should be clear whether the evidence is there, yes or no. I mean, I take it that your objection against violation of Rule 90(H)(ii) would be that some of the evidence would be stricken from the record. That's, I mean ... unless you had other ideas on what remedies would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, either stricken from the record, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or ignored? Or, I mean, if it's on the record, the Prosecution would --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Or -- well stricken from the record or that the Prosecution not be allowed to rely upon that evidence in particular ways, depending upon the way that they questioned the witness. For example, if they didn't put to the witness proposition A, they couldn't rely upon an answer he gave to support proposition A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see your point. At the same time, of course, it is a bit -- if you would do this only in -- during closing argument, for example, then, of course, it would be a bit late because at that moment it would be unclear for the Prosecution what they can rely upon or not because no ruling then has been made yet. So, therefore, whether -- your proposal, to say, Well, we do not insist on a ruling on Rule 90(H)(ii), but we keep it open to -- to -- to seek certain remedies at later stages, might, from a procedural point of view, create some problems. I suggest the following. At this moment, you're not insisting on a ruling. Could you please discuss with the Prosecution whether there are any elements remaining where you say, Well, this and this and this, you shouldn't use that, and then see to what extent you can agree with the Prosecution. If there's no agreement, then perhaps at a later stage it would be -- it would be clear to the Chamber what kind of remedy in respect of what portions of the evidence you're seeking. Rather than to wait until the final argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The problem I can foresee in that is as follows. That if the -- we don't object to the witness -- sorry, to the Prosecution investigators going to the witness's premises and taking those photographs, but we don't know what the Prosecution are going to say about the five individuals they cross-examined about. I don't think anyone in the courtroom could know what they're going to say about those five individuals, because they do not explain that position except that they were paid by the DB. But we don't know any -- much more than that. We don't know which operations they are alleged to have been a part of, and so on. Or what their criminal conduct, if any, was, or how that relates to the criminal purpose alleged against the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So perhaps you could at least start a conversation with the Prosecution in what respect they want to rely on the evidence of this witness in relation to those five persons. That's one. Second, apparently there's no objection at this moment against sending an investigator. I do not know -- it's -- it's -- the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I get some nice B/C/S on my English channel. There's no objection against sending an investigator. At the same time, the Chamber has not, at this moment, doesn't feel it of such importance that we would urge you to do that. But, of course, there's no objection. If you want at a later stage to show us that photograph, then we will consider that. But it's certainly, at this moment, it is not a -- something the Chamber considers of such importance that it -- that it either invites you or encourages you to do that. We leave it entirely in the hands of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, it is understood. In an abundance of caution, if the Prosecution does proceed, we do anticipate making arrangements through VWS just in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what was on my list remaining from last week. Anything else to be raised by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I raise an issue concerning Mr. Stanisic's health?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall that last week I indicated that Mr. Stanisic was attending the Bronovo hospital for the second round of treatment, the long-awaited treatment. Unfortunately, it appears that options have run out at the Bronovo hospital. Mr. Stanisic has been told that he cannot receive the second treatment because it would be too dangerous to his health to take the risk of, I think, allergic or other reactions. He has been told that the last option is surgery, surgery which is not possible in the Netherlands, but is available at the US -- in the USA, at the Cleveland Clinic, which apparently is the paramount clinic for this type of illness. Apparently Dr. van Geenen is going to write an official report following a telephone consultation next Thursday at 3.00 with Dr. Bo Shen in Cleveland and Mr. Stanisic's long-standing doctor, Dr. Tarabar from Belgrade. Things I -- we hope would be much clearer then. We would respectfully request that the Trial Chamber request an urgent report from a specialist, the reporting specialist dealing with this latest subject, this latest news. Yesterday we received answers from the reporting medical officer to the questions which we asked Your Honours to pose, and we're very grateful for those answers, answers which, as Your Honours know, we have not been able to obtain through the Registry from the treating doctors. And similarly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are talking about the specific questions the Chamber put to the reporting medical officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And the answers were extremely useful to us. We would, ideally, like to take the same route through the Registry and to the treating doctors with this latest subject, just to try to find out what precisely is the situation and the urgency of the treatment proposed. In light of the Registry's present position, or present position, we are not going to get answers to that -- to those questions via that route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're now talking about the questions in relation to the treatment -- the illness which triggered the need for this new medication and -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. In sum, we would say the best route for obtaining information which relates solely to Mr. Stanisic's treatment rather than the -- directly to the accused's fitness would be to go to his treating doctors. Unfortunately, the Registry do not take the same view. So what we're asking again is that the Court intervene to this degree to the extent that Your Honours would order the reporting specialist to report on this latest development. That serves two purposes: One, it provides us, or, rather, Mr. Stanisic with more detail; and, secondly, it would reassure, we hope, the Court, that Mr. Stanisic's ability to participate in the trial is not affected by this latest development. And for the avoidance of doubt, we're not suggesting at this stage that it does. We don't have the evidence to say that. But we do think, given the seriousness of this development, that caution is perhaps the best approach, and more information would be a wise course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, of course, the difference between the reporting on the matter where you had difficulties in obtaining information and the reporting on gastro-enterological problems was that we had a specialist-reporting doctor in that field, where we did not have any specialist reporting on psychological and psychiatric -- well, Dr. de Man, of course, but there was this conflict with the treating doctors. Now, wouldn't it be best that with seek an urgent report immediately after that contact this week, Thursday, has taken place, because then most likely we have the relevant information, and that we then specifically will ask the reporting specialist doctor to gain all the information from the treating doctors, including their communication with specialists in Cleveland, and then to receive a full overview of his opinion about that situation in terms of discontinuing the treatment in the Bronovo hospital, perhaps the Cleveland hospital as being the only one, or the best, for treatment, so that we formulate a few questions? If you have any suggestions, you may have noticed that the Chamber prefers to formulate the questions itself. We've done -- always done that because we are the ones who receive, first of all, the information. We are seeking it, first of all. But, of course, we are open to any suggestions. And you may have noticed that apparently what you were seeking in the recent past about the treatment on which you couldn't get the information that hopefully the Chamber included what you wanted to know in the questions it put to the -- to the reporting medical officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We completely agree that the right course would be to wait until this consultation. And perhaps the way for me to answer the second part is to say that there are some outstanding issues and we are -- but we're not going to concern the Trial Chamber with them at this stage. We're filing the motion to the President today concerning OLAD's position, but certainly the information that Your Honours elicited was extremely useful and we're extremely grateful for that intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll understand that what you'd like to know may be a mix of what Mr. Stanisic wants to know as a patient and what he wants to know so that it can be passed on to the Chamber as being relevant for the proceedings. And we try to make a clear distinction between the two so that we, especially, to the extent possible, will assist the Defence in receiving the information which, for the Chamber's relevance to receive for its purposes, and what is outside that scope, that we leave that to Defence and Registry or Defence and President or whomever is competent to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. And I hope that I've tried to also maintain that distinction, because I can see that distinction quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll consider -- if there is any input as far as questions are concerned, again, we may formulate them ourselves, we may impose certain limitations or even extensions, but if you, in whatever way, make that, your wishes, available to the Chamber, then we can consider them, because in view of the fact that it's Tuesday and when, Thursday, the communication between Cleveland and The Hague takes place, we would like to receive as soon as possible after that communication the information we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we'll send any questions, if we have them, by tomorrow, close of play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Marcus, usually the Office of the Prosecution does not intervene a lot, but -- on the manner, but you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's only to say we fully support what's taking place now. We would just welcome also the opportunity to put some proposed questions to the Chamber as we've done previously on many instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if we would stay within the same time-limits as the Defence indicated, that would be good.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the Simatovic, although it may have an impact on the proceedings at this moment, has no observations, or would you like to address the Chamber, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will have a position to state on this matter, but it is too soon now. As soon as we have sufficient information, we will inform you of our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simatovic [sic]. Then no other preliminaries. Then, in relation to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: -- there is one thing: There's a pending motion for protective measures from Serbia, and the Prosecution has a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was exactly why I had on my mind to go to private session. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I will re-start reading the decision of the Chamber. On the 23rd of January, 2012, Serbia requested protective measures for Witness DFS-017. Firstly, Serbia requests that the identity of the witness be protected. The request is denied. The witness is a former BIA operative, and Serbia has not sufficiently explained how public disclosure of his identity could give rise to a potential threat to Serbia's security interests. Secondly, Serbia requests that the witness be allowed to testify in closed session. Serbia argues that the witness will testify, and I quote, "in relation to nature, type, and intensity of the contacts he exchanged with Serbian MUP DB officials in the period from 1990 to 1995." Another quote: "Circumstances, facts, events and tasks pertaining to ..." and I leave out a certain portion, "his employment within the Serbian DB." And then last portion of the quote: "His knowledge regarding the co-operation with the Serbian DB and exchange of information and intelligence data and co-operation ..." and I again leave out a certain portion, "with the accused Franko Simatovic." The witness will be heard in open session, and the parties and the witness are now instructed to request provisional private session when their questions or the witness's answers might reveal, first, the identity of a BIA source; second, the identity of a BIA operative; or third, a location used by the BIA. Following the testimony of Witness DFS-017, the Registry will provide Serbia with the portions of transcripts of the testimony provisionally held in private session in order for them to request necessary redactions. And, Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to inform the Republic of Serbia of this decision. Mr. Petrovic, I -- you stated a minute ago that the witness is not seeking protective measures on his own behalf. Is that -- have you verified that recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked him about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's recent. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Draca. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. Could you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Draca. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, I'd like to inform you about a decision the Chamber delivered only a few minutes ago, a decision related to protective measures which were requested by the Republic of Serbia. Republic of Serbia had requested that you would testify in closed session and not under your own name but that your identity would be -- would not be disclosed to the public. That request has been denied. But where the Chamber has decided that you'll be heard in open session, you -- at the same time, your attention is drawn to the following. That when the questions or your answers might reveal, first, the identity of a BIA source, or, second, the identity of a BIA operative, or, three, a location used by the BIA, then we would turn into private session. The parties are instructed to notify the Chamber of such an event, and you are under a similar instruction. If your answers would reveal any of this information, we would then go into private session so that that information would not become public and that the Republic of Serbia later has an opportunity to review those portions of the testimony in order to further argue whether they should or should not necessarily be withheld from the public. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you'll now first be examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is, as you will be aware of, is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Petrovic has informed us that there were no personal reasons for you to seek protective measures in view of your own personal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Draca.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you first state your full name for the transcript, as well as your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Aco Draca. I was born in Sinj, the Republic of Croatia, on the 13th of December, 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, can you tell us what sort of educational background you have.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: I completed the high school in Benkovac and went on to get a degree in law from the Zagreb university.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you first took employment and where.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: In December of 1981, in the State Security Service, in the Zagreb centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what sort of duties you performed in your position for the state security in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: At the start of my career, I was first involved in secret surveillance and documentation, and after a while I was transferred to operative duties. I don't know if you're interested in the specific lines of work involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If need be, I will put specific questions to you. Witness, were you, at some point, relocated from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. In 1986, at my own request, I was transferred to the Split centre, the Zadar branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, the Zadar branch, under which structure did it fall; and how many workers did it have?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: As I said, it was the centre in Split, and it was the largest territorial centre in the former Yugoslavia, stretching all the way to Rijeka in the north and Montenegro in the south. There was Zadar, Sibenik, and Dubrovnik branches. I worked in Zadar. There were nine operatives in all, but we had other administrators, drivers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to tell us what activities you carried out when the political parties came to the political scene in the Republic of Croatia in 1989/1990?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for my professional engagements, I worked --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, just one moment. His Honour would like to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the interpreters are asking whether you would make a pause between question and answer and then between answer and question again, otherwise they will not be able to keep up with your speed of speech. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My professional engagement had to do with counter-intelligence vis-à-vis eastern European intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, at a certain point the political parties that were coming into being in 1989 and 1990, did they become the subject of interest of your service in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. In 1989, the multi-party system was introduced in the socialist Republic of Croatia as in all the former -- republics of the former SFRY, and then because of ethnic tensions that were becoming evident in that area the Split centre decided that all the operatives would exclusively cover the newly created parties in the sense of newly established extremists and possible terrorists' acts, violence. A large number of parties was founded. It was not even know what their objectives were. And if I may put it that way, it was just a democracy that was coming into being, and all nine of us who were working neglected all the other lines of work and covered exclusively the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, at this initial time when you received this instruction, were you covering political parties of all the peoples who were living in the territory that was covered by your branch?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Perhaps I didn't explain it in the best way. We didn't cover the political activities of those parties. Only those activities of those parties that had to do with potential terrorism and interethnic strife. There was only one party founded among the Serbian people, this is the Serbian Democratic Party, while the Croatian people had more parties, among whom the leading one was the Croatian Democratic Union headed by Dr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I also invite you to slow down slightly. Take a breath now and then so that the interpreters can do the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, at a certain point was this order changed as to the activities that were to be monitored and of which parties?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. I have to explain one more thing. According to the law that was in force at the time in Yugoslavia, there was some provisions referred to in citing ethnic intolerance and racial intolerance, and in the first orders the position of the SDB was to collect evidence, films, to document the activities which could be processed pursuant to that article of the criminal law. A few days, perhaps ten to 15 days before the first democratic elections in the Socialist Republic of Croatia, which is what it was at the time, an order came from Zagreb clearly stating that according to an order of the Central Committee of the Socialist Republic of Croatia the SDB must not put a hold to democratic processes in the country, and we were ordered to cease with these particular activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, was the activity suspended? Actually, can you first tell us what happened to the documentation that was compiled while you were working on the political parties in the previous period.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: We received an order from the Split centre to destroy the complete documentation which we organised on the same day. This was quite voluminous paper documentation and all the audio and video material from different meetings and encounters. That order was specific in one aspect as well, because it related exclusively to Croatian political parties. It did not refer to the Serbian Democratic Party. We continued to work on that with the explanation that extremism among the Serbian people could contribute to a growth in the conflict. And there was an order to fully devote ourselves to our work on the SDS so that at one point in time in Zadar we had a curious matter, where we were not working on Croatian nationalism, whereas we were working on Serbian nationalism. We had 12 actions in relation to people who were in the SDS. The curiosity was then that in that area the majority population was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we can very briefly talk about the situation in Zadar at the time and around the elections in 1990: What was the situation, were there any incidents, and what is the position of your service in relation to those incidents?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: The security situation was quite bad, especially after the elections which were won by the HDZ. Up until that time there was a hope that the SDP, the former communists headed by the late President Racan, would win the elections. They were much more mild. However, when the HDZ won the elections, interethnic tensions occurred and there was even an occurrence of the first Serbian Guards being formed in the Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you take it sentence by sentence and then make a very short break, that certainly would assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period, the first village guards were established at night in the Serbian villages exclusively. The Zadar area covered three municipalities other than Zadar. These were Beograd na Moru, Benkovac, and Obrovac. And Obrovac and Benkovac had a Serbian majority population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: I just wanted to add that in that period the service monitored everything that was happening in the field and was reporting back to Split and Zagreb about these nightguard duties as well. The JNA service was functioning also at the time and had joint meetings with representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army, or, rather, their security department. They undertook to go and visit those villages and to assure the people that there was no need for any guards because they were still guarantors of peace there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we will come to these questions. I would just like to ask you to try to focus on what I'm asking you and to -- so that we could present that the Trial Chamber in a brief and efficient manner. My question was: At this time in 1990 were there any incidents; and did your service interfere, did it react, to these incidents; and what was the information that it acquired?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: There were incidents, especially after the parliamentary elections which were won by the HDZ. Our direct instructions were, and it was partially a written instruction, not to interfere in the incidents but just to record them and to report on them. Not interference meant that we should not gather material evidence in order that these proceedings would be processed and so that criminal charges could be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, and what happened with the operatives in the DB of Serb ethnicity and also in the Split Police at this time, after the elections?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Shortly after the elections, or after the authorities were formed, the first multi-party authorities in Croatia, all the staff of DB received a loyalty document which they were obliged to sign. The document didn't indicate anything in particular, its content was similar to the ones we signed before about keeping state and professional secrets, other than the letterhead was changed. It was now the chequer-board. As for the other things, the -- the insignia, the first decision was to change the insignia on the hat and the sleeve. It was no longer the star, but the chequer-board. Some workers refused to that accept that insignia and they would get fired. In places like Knin and Benkovac, the staff continued to work but with old insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In one sentence, are you able to tell us why Serb staff refused to accept new insignia for their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Exclusively because the new insignia, in the form of the chequer-board, was almost identical to the insignia of the NDH from 1941, under whose administration over one million Serbs died in Croatia. So this associated them to that period, because the Serb population had suffered terribly under those symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, were there any new units being created at that time in the Croatian police; and if they were, who was joining those units?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. There were new units being created. The service's security assessment at this point in time -- well, I cannot say the service, but the Zadar branch, was that the establishment of these new units was considerably contributing to the tensions, because the old cadre of the public security service in the assessment of the Croatian leadership were not capable of covering the complete territory. President Tudjman made a decision to form -- President Tudjman made a decision to form special reserve forces of the police that would be mobilised exclusively from among the tough Croatian ethnic men, a vast majority of whom had a criminal record, in the area of Zadar where practically everybody knew each other. It was not a big place. We knew exactly who these people were. And this caused a lot of opposition even among the Croatian public. They got uniforms without any particular training. Camps were formed where these people were accommodated. Nobody knew what they were going to be used for, and this gave rise to fear in Serbian villages that one day or one night they would barge in and take over the police stations that were in the areas where the Serbs were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know about the 17th of August? Was there some sort of meeting scheduled in Benkovac? 17th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. This was in the outskirts of the village Bukovic, which is close to Benkovac. A meeting was scheduled and it was held. Professor Jovan Raskovic, president of the Serbian Democratic Party, convened a meeting for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did anything happen on the eve of that meeting, on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. On the evening before the meeting, in the evening of the 16th, sometime after midnight, a special unit from Zadar came to Benkovac, occupied the police station, broke down the door to the warehouse, because it was locked, and seized all the reserve forces' weapons, mostly long-barrelled weapons, automatic weapons, and they also seized the active forces' weapons which were being held there in case of some sort of emergency situation. At that time, they arrested and took with them the duty policemen whom they brought back the next day. That person was part of the Zadar police administration even though he was in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if there were any plans to carry out similar actions in other areas with Serb majority populations?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. A similar action was supposed to be carried out in smaller towns, like Obrovac, Gracac, and then Knin, as a larger centre, would have its turn, when it was surrounded and its police stations were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, how did you find out about the existence of these plans?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Because at that point in time I was still working, just like all of my colleagues were. Nobody had left at that point. We were coming to work. From time to time, our manager would inform us about plans, even though I have to emphasise that this was a time when most Serbs were going on sick-leave, were avoiding going to work, because we kept receiving, persistently, orders, especially Serbs, to cover Serbian territories. And so it would happen that you would submit a report as to what happened over the past week in the Benkovac or Obrovac area, then they - when I say "they," I'm thinking mostly of the leadership in Split and -- in Zadar and Zagreb - then they would say that we were minimizing Serbian activities. They would be skeptical.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break. Mr. Petrovic, until now we have heard a lot about the background, but I don't know to what extent it was explored with the Prosecution whether there is any disagreement, because I never felt that the Prosecution took a position that there was not rising ethnic tensions and administrative measures which might have considered to be against the Serbs in that area at that point in time. Perhaps you could use the break to find out. Because let's get as quickly as possible to what is the core of the testimony of this witness. And I take it it's not just background information. We take a break, and we resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you may proceed. But could I urge you and the witness to make pauses between question and answer and answer and question. And could I invite specifically the witness to slow down a bit because we would lose some of your words, which you would not wish to happen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, you have described the event in Benkovac of the 16th of August, 1990. Can you please tell us how the population reacted to the situation in the northern Dalmatia municipalities following these events. Was there something that happened out in the field?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. This event drastically changed the security situation in the field and heightened interethnic tensions. On the following morning, of the 17th of August, at this rally which had been scheduled earlier on, a great many citizens gathered because they had heard that the Benkovac SUP had had its weapons seized. Over 20.000 people attended the rally. News circulated of the Croatian police forces having used their helicopters to fly to Lika to seize weapons from the Serbian municipalities there. The information was confirmed by the JNA, and this was the first time that the JNA intervened and had its fighter planes up in the air to send the helicopters back. That was the first time that the population who gathered at the rally called on those present to issue them with weapons to protect themselves. The President of the SDS, Professor Jovan Raskovic, said at the rally that no weapons would be needed, that he would take it upon himself to speak to President Tudjman to prevent the conflict from escalating. Unfortunately, these words of reassurance didn't have the desired effect, and that very night roadblocks were erected with logs and all manner of other obstacles, severing all the various roads in the general area of Lika and the Cetina river.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, who erected these roadblocks; and who manned them?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: It was the local villagers who did. There were no roadblocks in Benkovac, but there were in all the villages around it. They mostly used hunting weapons and some of the trophy weapons that people still had from World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: One other question on this particular issue, Witness: Can you tell us, What was the Crystal Night in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: We are skipping onwards to 1991 now. I think it happened on the 4th of May. A day or two earlier, a Croatian reserve policeman was killed in the area between Benkovac and Zadar. The villagers of the village where the policeman hailed from organised a large protest rally in Zadar, and more than 10.000 people headed to destroy, on a rampage, to destroy everything that was owned by the Serbs - restaurants, bars. Even the open market stalls in Zadar that were owned by a Serb were destroyed. Every Serb that they came across in Zadar that day was lynched. People were injured. Quite a few stores and offices were set on fire, like, for instance, the Yugoslav Airlines offices as well as a number of other offices owned by companies from Belgrade who had their branches there. There were fires appearing across Zadar in some ten locations, and many people were out in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what happened to the Serb inhabitants in Zadar on the following day?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: That night in Zadar was a very difficult one for the Serbs. Nobody could sleep lest somebody should barge in their homes. And people would take off their name tags outside the front door so that nobody would know that they were Serbs. There were trucks pulling up in front of many homes, and many Serb inhabitants of Zadar left the town that day and headed for the areas where the majority of the Serbs lived. To describe the situation to you clearly: Zadar itself had some 100.000 inhabitants and of these, 25- to 30.000 were Serbs. The column that headed toward Benkovac and Knin of the Serbian refugees that day was endless. People were frightened, and they were frightened by that Crystal Night in Zadar, which got its name from the glass that had been smashed on the numerous window-panes and shop windows, and they were afraid of what might become of them. They were afraid to suffer that same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we mentioned the role of the JNA in 1990 and early 1991. Can you tell us, in that early period of the conflict what sort of reaction was there from the JNA with regard to the conflict and the roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: At the time, the Yugoslav People's Army wanted to enforce peace. At night they would not go to these roadblocks because they didn't want to heighten tensions, but in day-time they would go to Knin, Obrovac, and the nearby villages, and I mean the JNA officers. They would be visiting more prominent members of those communities, trying to persuade them to remove these roadblocks, saying that they would be the ones to guarantee peace as the army. They did the same by visiting Croatian villages. There were many villages with mixed population; half of them Serbs, half of them Croats. And then you would have JNA troops with armoured vehicles standing guard round the clock to make sure that no individuals would be able to cause any incidents that would inflame the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: These buffer zones between Croat and Serb villages that you've just been referring to served, in fact, to form a line of separation between Serb-inhabited areas and Croat-inhabited areas, if my understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Well, I can't really call it a line of separation. There were several APCs, several soldiers, mostly of the military police. They would go from village to village. In some areas where relations were good, they were more successful. In others, less. You can't call it a line of separation, really. There were literally a couple of patrols trying to make sure that no incidents occur between the two peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: While the JNA was playing the role that you've just described, were there instances of Croat villages being taken by Serb forces or Serb villages being taken by Croat forces? Or ...

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: No. Not in that period of time. No areas were taken. There were no major provocations or acts of aggression on either side. There weren't even instances of either Croats or Serbs leaving these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know whether in the summer of 1991 there occurred a change in the personnel of the JNA commands and units in the area?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a change in that the JNA was being understaffed because a great many officers and soldiers started leaving the JNA ranks and joining the Croatian side. At this time, the national corps guard -- National Guard Corps was being set up and the Croatian authorities were calling on everyone to leave the JNA ranks and join the National Corps Guard [as interpreted]. And these events came to a head in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, was there a shift in the attitude on the part of the Croatian authorities towards the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes, there was a major shift. In July and especially in August, after President Tudjman and the Croatian authorities called on the army to withdraw from Croatian towns, the General Staff of the army rejected the ultimatum and suggested that the political situation be resolved -- that the situation be resolved through political means. I think that once a month the presidents of all the various republics met in order to agree on the political future of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, witness, I'm interrupting you, but could you focus on my question. In the area where you were, was there a shift in terms of how the Croatian authorities regarded the JNA; and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. An order was issued for the barracks to be placed under blockade. I can't say that it was just the MUP and the National Guards Corps, but at any rate there was a call for the barracks to be placed under a blockade. And when I say "under a blockade," that their water and electricity supplies should be severed and that they should be physically blocked as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many barracks there were in Zadar and what became of them in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: There were three major barracks in Zadar and several smaller ones, and they were all placed under a blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like us to discuss now your particular movements at the time. Did there come a time when you came in touch with the MUP of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this was and who with?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: It was in late Autumn or early winter of 1990. My assumption at the time was that we would all have to leave Zadar one day or another, and I got in touch with the Benkovac Police Station and discussed the possibility of me joining their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet Milan Martic at some point?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. It was a briefing. It was shortly after that first meeting in the SUP of Benkovac. The commander of the Benkovac SUP took me to meet Milan Martic in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Martic tell you of some of his ideas about forming institutions in the area of Krajina at this point?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. It was a long discussion, more than an hour. I knew that the area which was called the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina at the time did not have a security infrastructure when it comes to state security. It didn't have either the personnel, officers, equipment, or anything else, because in what was then the Socialist Republic of Croatia these regions were covered by centres located in major towns. Martic did confirm to me that they did not have a security structure branch but that would the situation be developing in the direction of them having to resist the new government in Zagreb, he would be planning to set up a State Security Service for Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the SAO Krajina, were there any state security professionals from the pre-war service?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: No. I should clarify this a bit perhaps. The Kordun area was covered by Karlovac. Banija was covered by Sisak. For instance, Knin was covered by Sibenik. Benkovac and Obrovac were covered by Zadar. As I said, these small towns didn't have either the personnel or the offices. However, in the town of Knin there were two operatives who would be visiting on occasion from Sibenik, but they would be using the premises of the SUP of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was a decision taken at some point to form a State Security Service of the SAO Krajina? And if so, do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. With the negative developments that followed - when I say "negative," I mean in terms of peace - a body was established in Knin called the Serb National Council which took care of negotiations and anything that had to do with the region. They decided that the ministry of the police should be set up as part of the Serbian National Council. I don't think they called it ministry at the time at all. It was called the Krajina Police. I was in touch with Martic at that point. That was just on the new year's eve of 1990, because it was on the 5th of January that Martic officially issued the decision to set up the Krajina Police, so the meeting must have taken place ahead of the 5th of January, and he introduced me to Dusan Orlovic who he said was charged with running the State Security Service in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did Dusan Orlovic have any experience in the DB area of work?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: No. He had never worked at the police before or in the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At some point did Orlovic give you any assignments?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: At the beginning there were no particular tasks other than the general tasks to compile data relating to the threats to the area around Benkovac because of the special units of the Croatian MUP so that we could alert the inhabitants of the villages in time to get ready for defence or evacuation. I must emphasise that in that period the JNA still existed. And when I say "ours," I mean our Serbian population in that area. So our hopes were that the army would secure peace. But if this did not happen, we had to prepare in a way, in the event of an attack, to be able to inform the inhabitants of the village so that they could withdraw to be safe. Because, at that time still there were no adequate weapons for them to be able to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, at some point was there a -- a branch of the state security that was established in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. That's why I said earlier that these were initial assignments. And then in late winter/early spring 1991, I was given an order to form an SDB branch in Benkovac, to pick my own personnel, seven to eight operatives, and he also informed me about the organisational chart. He also said that the other areas in the Krajina area were also setting up branches in the same way, and we all were linked to the Knin centre, which at that point in time was under his leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in that period, in 1991, what were the work conditions in the State Security Service of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Well, it was a total improvisation. Literally. There were no typewriters, never mind any more advanced technical equipments or the ability to be able to perform analysis or do any basic tasks. The main task then was also to gather information about threats to the inhabitants of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And, witness, are you aware as to how the state security of Krajina was financed in that period?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: The Krajina State Security Service was being financed in the same way as the public security service, in the identical way. It was a decision by the Serb National Council, or, rather, they appealed to the citizens to help different individuals and businesses who wanted to give donations. All policemen, regardless of their rank, position, their work, they all were receiving an identical salary at that time from that same fund.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And, sir, who led the State Security Service of Krajina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Dusan Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us - if you know - if the service received instructions and directives for its work in that period? And if it did, who did they come from?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Judging by the meetings that I had with Orlovic in Knin quite frequently in that period, because there was no other communication, we had to submit all our reports by messenger -- I'm sorry, can you please repeat specifically what your question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question was this: Who did the service in -- receive its instructions and directives from in that period? If it did.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Orlovic informed me that it was exclusively from the Serbian National Council. But it was known that Martic also had a certain influence over that. At the time, the council changed its name to the Council for National Defence, so it was the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in 1991, how did Milan Martic evaluate the work of the Krajina State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: In the beginning, the reporting to Martic indicated that he was quite satisfied, but then as the year evolved he was less and less satisfied. We had a several -- several meetings where he objected to the quality of the work, meaning that he was not satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did the SDB at any point cease to exist? The SDB Krajina.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. Martic made a decision to dissolve the service in late November/early December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was this decision implemented?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I just have a few questions now about an earlier period and on a different topic, but I think this is a good place to put those questions to you. Do you know how the first weapons were received in Benkovac? How and when.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: The first weapons that arrived in Benkovac - and I was personally informed about this action, if I may call it like that - there was considerable pressure from inhabitants of villages bordering on Croatian villages towards Zadar. The JNA at the time refused to distribute weapons to arm and mobilise the village population. Since Benkovac had a TO but did not have its own depots, at a number of meetings in Knin and written proposals to the Serb National Council it was indicated that the population was threatened by the Croatian forces in these border areas, so the council made a decision and from the TO Golubic depot in Knin they took old weapons, carbines, old Russian weapons from World War II, machine-guns, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned the TO Golubic depot. What kind of facility is this, this depot in Golubic? Can you describe it? Who ran the facility, where is it located?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: The depot is close to the village of Golubic, some 15 kilometres from Knin, in the direction of Bosnia. This is believed to be one of the largest depots in the central Dalmatia area. It's under the control of the JNA. A smaller part of the depot was used by the TO. This was a decision dating from the 1960s, when the TO system was established. So a part of that depot was given for the use of the TO, and that depot mostly had old weapons to be used by the TO reserved forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this -- these weapons, this initial quantity of weapons that arrived in Benkovac, how was this distributed? Whom was it given to?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: The local commune presidents came from those villages, and then it was decided that the weapons should go there. I don't know -- I know the names of the villages. I don't know if that means anything to the Trial Chamber. These people came. Since no institution took it upon itself to distribute the weaponry - there was no war yet, the JNA still existed as a cohesive force in the field, although there were threats, but there were no lines, there was no -- there were no clashes - so the initial quantities of the weapons were distributed to representatives of the local communes, at the entrance to Benkovac, in a pine forest, according to a list which wasn't very long. It was about ten rifles that were issued per village. The action was conducted by a representative -- or by the representative of the Knin TO in co-operation with the commander of the Benkovac TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the TO Benkovac representative. Do you know the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. It's Milan Dragisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know Zdravko Zecevic, a person by the name of Zdravko Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, in 1991, whether this person had any duties that they were carrying out in the SAO Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Zdravko Zecevic is from the same place that I am. I know him from my childhood. In 1990 he joined the SDS party, and he was the first president of the Benkovac municipality because that party won the elections in Benkovac. At the same time, he was the vice-president of the SDS party. He was the vice-president to President Jovan Raskovic and a member of the Serbian National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In May 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question to clarify one of the previous answers of the witness. The decision to use some of the TO weaponry from the Golubic depot and to distribute that, could you give that a date or an approximately -- an approximate date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was in early May 1991, after the Zadar Crystal Night. This was then approximately on the 10th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, Zecevic was the president of the Benkovac municipality. Did Mr. Zecevic summon you to a meeting in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Zecevic frequently called me to meetings that mostly -- because he personally believed that he completely was out of his depth in security areas. He would often ask for my security assessments. So I don't know which meeting you mean. We had a lot of meetings in April as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zecevic call you to a meeting to meet some people who had arrived in the Krajina area in April or May 1991? People from outside who were not from Benkovac or from the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Ah, yes, now I know which meeting you mean now. The meeting took place in April, not in May. He called me and said that he would like me to attend the meeting with him because a particular man was coming about whom he didn't know anything. He asked me if I knew anything about him. This was Captain Dragan that he was talking about. At that point I didn't know of this man. I met him for the first time at this meeting with Zecevic. This happened in early April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did Zecevic want you to see Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: He told me himself that he felt on uncertain ground there, that he didn't know this Captain Dragan. He was told that this was a man who was a high-ranking officer of the Australian army, with excellent connections with many security companies in the United States, in Ireland, throughout the world, so he didn't feel sure of himself, and he suggested that I wait for this man together with him, who was coming upon the recommendation of his friends from Belgrade and from the Serbian diaspora, especially from the United States, and simply to help him to evaluate this man as a person. To put it briefly, he was afraid that perhaps this was some kind of crook, because in that period people like that did come to the Krajina area an offer their services.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Other than this meeting, this first meeting, were there any other meetings that you attended between Captain Dragan and Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. After three to four weeks - this was already May - there was a second meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who attended this second meeting?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Zecevic called me in the same way, and he said that Captain Dragan was coming again but this time he was in the company of Martic. He also insisted that I attend that meeting, and this did take place in May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And at that time did Martic say anything about Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Yes. He was quite taken by him. He was full of praise for him. He said that he was a man who could help, because a problem cropped up at the time. It was a process that took a while, and that was the departure of all the Croatian cadres from all the Krajina police stations. So there was a need for somebody to make up those missing staff, and Captain Dragan could do that. Martic said that he could facilitate a course of infantry training, and if any war broke out, this police force would have basic police skills. And Martic told Zecevic and myself that Captain Dragan was going to be taking this course, that he was actually going to be organising a course in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you know, why did Martic come to Zecevic to talk about the topic of Captain Dragan and the setting up of this infantry course that you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Well, the first thing is that Martic, in that period, had a lot of respect for Zecevic as an intellectual, a very calm and capable man and politician. Secondly, through Zecevic the first contact was established with Martic. So I don't know exactly who these people are. Perhaps I knew their names at the time, but they didn't mean anything to me. I don't know who it was who came to Zecevic with Captain Dragan and then told him about Martic. So Martic knew Zecevic had a lot of connections in the Serbian diaspora, throughout the world, and he wanted him to help in the sense of putting out the word in the world that Captain Dragan was setting up this camp, that assistance was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but it says here in line 47 -- on page 47, line 6 and 7, that Zecevic set up the first contact with Martic. Is that what you said or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Zecevic set up the first contact of Captain Dragan with Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Draca, what was your impression about Captain Dragan on the basis of the contacts you had with him?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning it was completely positive. He was a very energetic man and he wasn't an extremist, which I liked. He did not mention any extremists or, if I may freely say so, pro-Chetnik attitudes. But as time went by, my opinion changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you say that your opinion changed. Why did you change it?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA
utterances.text: Well, considering my job at the time, that is to say, collecting information, I was well aware of what was happening in the area of all villages in the vicinity of Benkovac and Knin. And I noticed that Captain Dragan came on his own initiative, without agreements with anyone from the Serbian authorities, the Serbian National Council, or police, or the army. He would come on his own. He would hold rallies. He would try to cause a rebellion of the people against the army. He claimed that he was the only one who could save the Krajina and that he could only save Krajina one day when the JNA toppled, because that was what he foresaw. He would also slander the local politicians and he would cause unrest in a way. The simple-minded people who were afraid of a possible Croatian attack did not see him in such a way. He was accepted wherever he went. There would be euphoria in every village. I could feel, however, that that was not good in the overall context for the unity of the people in the area. He was spending less and less time at the camp. At one point, I even asked Orlovic whether he knew what was happening and why, if his position was to train the police in the camp, he wasn't doing his job. And then - I may have missed to say this - he brought another foreign citizen, whose name was Mark Lynch; he was an Irishman. He would most often leave him in the camp and he would wonder around the area.
